claims.text: The tribo-corrosion response of high-entropy alloys is governed by mechanical removal of a protective passivating oxide during sliding.
The initial alloy surface has a native, conformal, protective passivating oxide layer.
Sliding locally disrupts and thins the protective oxide at wear tracks.
Mechanical oxide removal exposes fresh underlying alloy to the corrosive electrolyte.
Freshly exposed alloy surfaces undergo accelerated localized anodic dissolution.
Freshly exposed surfaces repassivate slowly and non-uniformly.
Defective or thin oxide coverage enhances anodic dissolution.
Defective or thin oxide coverage reduces wear resistance.
The interaction of oxide disruption and imperfect repassivation produces synergistic degradation under simultaneous wear and corrosion.
Combined sliding and corrosion will produce a significantly higher total degradation rate than dry mechanical wear alone.
Combined sliding and corrosion will produce a significantly higher total degradation rate than static corrosion alone.
The combined condition will have increased corrosion current density relative to the single-action controls.
The combined condition will produce deeper wear tracks than the relevant wear-only control.
The combined condition will produce rougher wear tracks than the relevant wear-only control.
The predicted response holds when mechanical oxide removal is faster than oxide reformation.
Extremely rapid repassivation can suppress the predicted synergistic response.
High-oxygen environments can promote sufficiently rapid oxide formation to make the prediction fail.
The predicted response may fail when corrosive species are absent or negligible.
Microstructural heterogeneity may modify the relative contributions of oxide removal and repassivation.

contradictions.description: The conditions state that an identical corrosive environment applies to all tests, but the proposed controls include dry wear, inert-electrolyte wear, and static immersion in a corrosive electrolyte, which necessarily do not share an identical corrosive environment.

The main comparison defines the mechanical-only baseline as dry sliding, whereas the falsification experiment substitutes sliding in an inert electrolyte. These are not matched controls because the liquid can alter lubrication, friction, and wear.
